source.title: Revisiting the Arcade Learning Environment: Evaluation Protocols and Open Problems for General Agents

accepted.question_text: How can an agent in the Arcade Learning Environment automatically learn a generic internal representation that works across many Atari 2600 games, while being much more sample-efficient than current DQN-like methods, avoiding heavy task-specific tuning, and coping with sparse-reward games such as Montezuma’s Revenge where current methods may occasionally encounter reward without learning to obtain it consistently?

evidence.quote: The latter is obviously more desirable for the potential of discovering better representations while alleviating the burden of having handcrafted features.

However, reinforcement learning methods based on neural networks still have a high sample complexity, requiring at least dozens of millions of samples before achieving good performance, in part due to the need for learning this representation.
This suggests that there is still room for significant progress on effectively learning good representations in the ALE.

accepted.question_text: How can one learn and use a model of Atari 2600 games in the Arcade Learning Environment that stays accurate over long rollouts, is fast enough to be useful for planning rather than slower than the emulator itself, and still supports effective planning when the learned model is imperfect and errors compound over time?
accepted.context_brief: Planning and learned models in ALE

evidence.quote: so far, there has been no clear demonstration of successful planning with a learned model in the ALE.
In both cases, however, the models are much slower than the emulator itself; designing a fast, accurate model remains an open problem.
A related open problem is how to plan with an imperfect model.

accepted.question_text: How can a model-free reinforcement learning agent with function approximation explore the Arcade Learning Environment efficiently enough to discover rewards that are delayed, sparse, or initially negative, as in games such as Montezuma’s Revenge, Private Eye, Pitfall!, and Tennis, potentially by committing to temporally extended decisions at a higher level of abstraction than individual joystick moves and by using intrinsic motivation when scoring appears impossible?
accepted.context_brief: Exploration under sparse or deceptive rewards

evidence.quote: In several games such as Montezuma’s Revenge and Private Eye (see Figure 6) even obtaining any feedback is difficult because thousands of actions may be required before a first positive reward is seen.

However, despite successes in individual games, such as Bellemare et al.’s success in Montezuma’s Revenge, none of these approaches has been able to improve, in a meaningful way, agents’ performance in games such as Pitfall!, where the only successes to date involve some form of apprenticeship

An aspect that still seems to be missing are agents capable of committing to a decision for extended periods of time, exploring in a different level of abstraction, something that humans frequently do.

Finally, for intrinsically difficult games, agents may need some form of intrinsic motivation (Oudeyer, Kaplan, & Hafner, 2007; Barto, 2013) to keep playing despite the apparent impossibility of scoring in the game.

accepted.question_text: How can an Arcade Learning Environment agent transfer knowledge across Atari games so as to reduce the number of samples needed to learn new games, including games that are only loosely analogous, while automatically determining when transfer is beneficial versus when it causes negative transfer, and while separating representation transfer from policy transfer instead of conflating both inside a single expert-pretrained neural-network approach?

evidence.quote: We can expect knowledge transfer to reduce the required number of samples needed to learn to play similar games.
A more ambitious research question is how to leverage general video game experience, sharing knowledge across games that are not directly analogous.
It is not clear how this should be addressed in the ALE. Ideally one would like to have an algorithm automatically deciding which games are helpful and which ones are not.

Finally, current approaches are only based on the use of neural networks to perform transfer, conflating representation and policy transfer. It may be interesting to investigate how to transfer each one of these entities independently.

accepted.question_text: How can one obtain an off-policy reinforcement learning method for the Arcade Learning Environment that is both stable and practical under function approximation, has theory that actually explains its empirical behavior, can reliably reuse samples generated by policies very different from the current one, and does not depend on brittle heuristics such as replay buffers or target networks merely to avoid divergence?

evidence.quote: Off-policy learning algorithms seem to be brittle when applied to the ALE.

However, besides a better theoretical understanding about convergence, stable (and practical) off-policy learning algorithms with function approximation are still an incomplete piece in the literature.

Addressing the aforementioned issues, either through a convincing demonstration of the efficacy of the current theoretically sound algorithms for off-policy learning, or through some of the improvements described above may free us from the increased complexity of using experience replay and/or target networks.
Also, this would allow us to better reuse samples from policies that are very different from the one being learned.
